cells.tense: Right now you are checking the next question against the last answer.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Choose the direction you have been circling, and make one move on it this week without consulting anyone first — one call, one booking, one pencil line under it.
cells.core:
You turn things over, compare what you find, and the directions you commit to tend to hold. When something is explained to you, you listen past the surface and measure it against what you already trust. That measuring is how you choose, and it has been carrying you well.

What this stretch is free to feed next is a decision that moves. There is a direction you have been examining from several angles — you have enough. Take one action that only happens if you have picked it: send the message, book the thing, write the date down. Curiosity brought you to the fork, and the step is the part curiosity cannot take for you. Do the one thing and notice whether the ground under it holds as you expected.
cells.sheetLine: You think your way to the fork, and the step is still yours.
cells.verb: turning things over until they make sense — asking, comparing, staying curious past the first answer
cells.place: at the desk where a direction is picked and kept

cells.tense: You will have it all worked out before anything has actually started.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin something small with no destination yet — the first move only — and go looking for what it grows into.
cells.core:
You are running the options so thoroughly that the first move keeps being postponed. Every branch gets explored, every consequence weighed, and the person who is supposed to walk into the deciding is already braced for a meeting that has not been called. The asking that should open a path is covering the path — the exploring has gone long enough to crowd out the moving.

Try starting while still curious. Begin something small that could genuinely be yours, on the strength of the starting — the draft, the class, the first call. Nothing needs to be settled about where it goes. The question research cannot answer is what a direction feels like once it is underway, and only moving answers it. Keep the thing smaller than it will become.

cells.tense: You stopped at the fork with good questions and stayed there.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: First thing each morning, sense how one choice might feel a month after it is made — first impression, nothing to fix, no decision owed.
cells.core:
The questions come slower than they used to, and when they come, they land flat. You sit at the point where a direction gets picked, circling the same few options, and none of them pulls. The effort is still there. What ran out is the something ahead worth moving toward.

Being told to decide harder will not bring it back. Wonder will. Each morning, before the day gets loud, sense how one of the choices might feel a month after it is made — lighter, heavier, unfinished. You are not deciding anything. You are letting the future do the pulling, and a mind given something to look forward to starts perceiving again. The direction comes back through the sensing, not through the force.

cells.tense: You are choosing all day and describing it as mostly going along.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: When a choice stirs something in you, weigh that feeling once before deciding — what it is for and what it costs — then decide on the scales.
cells.core:
The decisions are happening and most of them hold. What is missing from the account is the fact that they are yours. Ask what you want and you will say you have not worked it out; describe the day and it sounds like drift. The steering is quiet and steady, and the part of it you have ruled out is what you feel about each choice.

When a choice stirs something, do the weighing yourself before you move — what this feeling is asking for, what it would cost to give it. One look at the scales, then decide. Being fair to a feeling is not obeying it, and saying it once inside is enough for the choice to stop looking like something that happened to you. What you decide will hold better for having been weighed.
cells.sheetLine: The choices are steady, and yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person deliberately steers by what they know, when the record only shows the knowing is happening — authorship of the direction is exactly what is unacknowledged. A reader could say 'I do choose, I just can't always say how I chose — and that's fine.' The ask survives being wrong: asking one beginner's question and staying with the answer until something moves is a real experiment in direction whatever the reader's account of themselves turns out to be. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'You already know what to do' — it flatters the card, it explains nothing, and it hands them an answer instead of a step; it is gone from all four cells.

A reader could reasonably object that they know exactly how they choose and simply don't narrate it — and the ask still stands in that case, since naming what a choice stirs before deciding is a small experiment either way. The sentence that serves the writer more than them was 'The direction is real, and it carries your signature' — it flatters the frame and tells them nothing they can use. Gone. The four acts now open on four different verbs (cut, start, sense, make), and only one carries a clock.
